**Video:** [Lec 09 — Density Function](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=_QrezNPmxDk)

### Learning goals
- Define a **probability density function** (PDF) for a continuous RV
- Remember: PDF value at a point is **not** a probability
- Contrast with discrete **probability mass functions** (PMFs)
- Reframe ML as estimating densities (when they exist)

### Before this clicks
The **distribution / CDF** $P_{X}$ is a probability measure on (Borel) sets — the pushforward of $P$. Densities are a convenient description of many continuous laws, not a replacement for the idea of measure.

---

## 1. Definition (continuous case)

Let $X$ be continuous with distribution (CDF) $P_{X}$. A **density** $p_{X}$ is a function

$$
p_{X}:\ \text{range of }X\ \to\ [0,\infty)
$$

such that (in 1D)

$$
P_{X}(x)=\int_{-\infty}^{x} p_{X}(t)\,dt
$$

when this makes sense. In $\mathbb{R}^{D}$, the same idea uses a $D$-dimensional integral over the “southwest” region used for the multivariate CDF.

**Properties to lock in:**

- Densities are **non-negative**.
- They are **not** required to lie in $[0,1]$.
- $\int p_{X}=1$ over the whole space (normalization).

Course notation habit (approximate): fancy / double-stroke $P$ for distributions; plain $p$ for densities. From here on, algorithms mostly manipulate **densities**.

---

## 2. Evaluating a density $\neq$ getting a probability

Plug a number $x_0$ into $p_{X}$: you get a non-negative real number. That number is **not** $P(X=x_0)$ in continuous models.

Probabilities come from **integrating** the density over a set:

$$
P(X\in A)=\int_{A} p_{X}(x)\,dx.
$$

Integrals over regions recover the distribution (a true probability measure). Point evaluations do not.

People still call $p_{X}(x_0)$ a **likelihood** (of the parameter / model at that observation) — useful language later, still not “probability of the singleton.”

---

## 3. Interview trap: uniform on $[0,1/2]$

If $X\sim\mathrm{Uniform}[0,1/2]$, then

$$
p_{X}(x)=2\quad\text{for }x\in[0,1/2].
$$

The density equals **2**, which cannot be a probability (probabilities $\le 1$). Yet

$$
\int_{0}^{1/2} 2\,dx=1,
$$

so as a density it is perfectly valid. This kills the myth “PDF values are probabilities because Gaussians look $\le 1$.”

---

## 4. Discrete case: mass functions

For a **discrete** RV, the object analogous to a density is a **probability mass function** (PMF). Evaluating a PMF at a point **is** a probability:

$$
p_{X}(x)=P(X=x).
$$

Same letter $p$ is often overloaded — always ask: continuous or discrete?

Not every continuous law has a density (pathological cases exist). In this course we assume practical data can be modeled with RVs that **do** have densities.

---

## 5. Problem statement, updated

Earlier: given $\mathcal{D}$, estimate the **distribution**.

Working form from now:

$$
\text{Given }\mathcal{D},\ \text{estimate the density }p\quad
\text{(joints / marginals / conditionals as needed)}.
$$

We speak of distributions when we mean the probability measure; we **compute** with densities for mathematical ease, assuming a one-to-one link in the well-behaved cases we care about.

---

## 6. Tiny concrete example

Let

$$
p(x)=\begin{cases}6x(1-x), & 0\le x\le 1,\\ 0, & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}
$$

Check normalization:

$$
\int_{0}^{1}6x(1-x)\,dx=6\int_{0}^{1}(x-x^{2})\,dx=6\Bigl[\tfrac{1}{2}-\tfrac{1}{3}\Bigr]=1.
$$

Then $p(0.5)=6\cdot 0.5\cdot 0.5=1.5$, which is fine for a density, **not** a probability. But

$$
P(0.4\le X\le 0.6)=\int_{0.4}^{0.6}6x(1-x)\,dx
$$

**is** a probability.

---

## 7. Common confusions

| Confusion | Clarification |
|-----------|----------------|
| $p(x)\in[0,1]$ always | False — see uniform on a short interval. |
| $p(x_0)=P(X=x_0)$ continuously | False for continuous RVs. |
| Density = distribution | Density *describes* many continuous distributions; the distribution is the measure / CDF. |
| No density $\Rightarrow$ useless data | Rare pathologies; we assume nice densities exist for our data. |
